extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing comedy critics, entertainment journalists, and reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for critics who review and cover comedy (stand-up, specials, club scenes, and related media), focusing on how to write for audiences, justify the critic's role, and evaluate comedy within cultural and technological context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify your existence / focus on readers
rubrics_metrics.description: You have to justify your existence as a critic; your central concern should be what’s good or bad for your readers (not necessarily for comedians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because media is democratized and many ordinary opinions exist, a critic's value is putting work in context and adding perspective readers can't get from casual viewers. Ask yourself 'What purpose am I serving here?' and make your reviews serve reader needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for both novices and experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep in mind 'that audience member who watches only one special a year' while also serving readers who know the tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance accessibility and depth: don't merely offer an ordinary civilian's opinion; provide context and analysis that enriches a novice's understanding while still engaging more informed readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide broader contextual connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring a wealth of experience to make connections to broader political, moral, historical, or aesthetic context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical parallels, political framing, and aesthetic lineage to situate a comedian's work within traditions and movements — this is a primary way critics add value beyond casual opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be both incredibly arrogant and incredibly humble
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic needs arrogance to think others should listen, but that arrogance must be earned; simultaneously, be open to the best argument against you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earn authority through hard work, study, and thinking; remain open-minded so you don't become a 'calcified, boring writer.' It's a constant struggle to balance confidence and humility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show up consistently — attend many shows to predict trends
rubrics_metrics.description: If you just show up enough, if you go to enough shows, you can predict the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular attendance and immersion in the scene lets critics spot emerging trends and new voices; consistent presence provides foresight that casual observers lack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to take strong positions and accept criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: One of our jobs is to be the 'clown in the dunking booth.' We should be able to take criticism — take a strong position and invite opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taking decisive stands is valuable because it provokes debate and helps shape discourse; critics should tolerate pushback and learn from it rather than avoid contention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid résumé-style repetition of past works; focus on what's on stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience can become a negative when a critic treats reviews as a catalogue of past examples (e.g., writing about the 50 other Hamlets you'd seen instead of what’s on stage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize acute, present-focused description and analysis of the specific work at hand rather than relying on long lists of previous comparisons that distract from current observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with pushback in a democratized media environment
rubrics_metrics.description: When media is democratized, critics must engage with critiques of their role and power (e.g., concerns that a critic's negative review could harm careers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should acknowledge legitimate pushback, explain their purpose publicly, and be transparent about their methods and standards to justify their authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit mistakes and revise interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics will get things wrong and should acknowledge changes in opinion (e.g., re-evaluating a 'comedy boom is going to bust' thesis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to reframe past pieces in light of new evidence or shifting contexts; explain what you got wrong and why to maintain credibility and intellectual honesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for technological and platform shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that current changes in comedy are driven by technology and platforms (making clubs and alt rooms less central) rather than only historical factors like real estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame coverage to reflect how platforms, distribution, and tech affect careers and forms of comedy; avoid anachronistic explanations that ignore digital/technological drivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curiosity is a core requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Curiosity about new spins, framings, and how comedians think through ideas is central to doing the job well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain an appetite for novelty and the intellectual pleasure of seeing someone develop a comedic idea; this fuels sustained, engaged criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experience judiciously; don’t let it calcify your perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience can be valuable but can also blind you or lead to stale writing if it becomes a reflexive catalogue of past works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage experience to deepen analysis but guard against overreliance on it; prioritize fresh observation and be open to being surprised by new approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of the critic’s potential power over careers
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize critiques that claim a critic could wield excessive influence over comedians' careers and be conscious of that responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance honest evaluation with awareness of real-world effects; engage with community concerns and avoid wielding authority without accountability.
